cards.front: In young children pleural effusions are hard to distinguish from other hazy shadowing because most films are taken [___], so fluid layers posteriorly.
cards.context:
Why effusions are harder to call in small children, and it is about positioning rather than the fluid.

Most paediatric films are taken supine, so fluid layers posteriorly instead of collecting at the base. The result is a hazy hemithorax that is difficult to separate from consolidation.

cards.front: In cystic fibrosis, the defective cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel produces thick, [___] airway secretions; impaired mucociliary clearance drives chronic infection and progressive bronchiectasis.
cards.context:
CFTR normally exports chloride into airway lumen, drawing water with it to keep mucus hydrated for cilial clearance.

Once bronchiectasis develops, the cycle is self-sustaining.

cards.front: Universal newborn hearing screen target ages: screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months, intervene by [___] months — closes the critical window for language development.
cards.context:
The 1-3-6 rule for newborn hearing screening: screen by 1 month (OAE first-line, ABR for NICU), confirm any failed screen with audiology by 3 months. Start intervention (hearing aids, early-intervention) by 6 months.

The targets aren't arbitrary — the first 6 months are the critical language-scaffolding window, and delays past it measurably impair lifelong speech outcomes.

In Australia ~98% are screened by 1 month; compliance falls off at diagnosis and intervention, which is where infants slip through.

cards.front: Epiglottitis is classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b — rare now due to vaccination; child is toxic, drooling, in [___] posture.
cards.context:
Hib epiglottitis was once common in 2-7 year olds but has been nearly eliminated by routine Hib vaccination. Now consider it in unvaccinated children, immigrants, and unusual organisms (Group A Strep, S. aureus).

Tripod posture (sitting forward with neck extended, mouth open) optimises airway patency in the face of supraglottic obstruction.

cards.front: A febrile infant aged 28 days or younger needs full evaluation + [___] for empirical IV antibiotics even if well-appearing.
cards.context:
Any infant aged 28 days or younger by corrected age with fever ≥38°C or hypothermia <36°C needs admission, a serious-bacterial-infection workup and prompt empirical IV antibiotics, even if well.

Obtain blood culture, catheter/SPA urine and, unless contraindicated, CSF. Appearance is unreliable because neonates may not localise or contain infection.

RCH empiric therapy: ≤48 hours after birth, benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; >48 hours without meningitis, cefazolin plus gentamicin. Suspected meningitis needs benzylpenicillin plus a third-generation cephalosporin.

cards.front: Pubertal gynaecomastia affects ~[___]% of normal males in Tanner stages 3-4; usually resolves spontaneously within 1-2 years.
cards.context:
Pubertal gynaecomastia affects up to 80% of normal males in Tanner stage 3-4 — transient relative oestrogen excess as testosterone production rises.

Refer if persistent (>2 years), severe, or features of underlying pathology (Klinefelter, drug use, sex steroid tumour).

cards.front: Management of typical D+ haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is [___] — antibiotics are contraindicated as they may increase toxin release.
cards.context:
Typical (D+) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from EHEC, usually O157:H7. Toxin binds glomerular endothelial Gb3 receptors → thrombotic microangiopathy; haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia.

Antibiotics are contraindicated (release more toxin, worsen outcomes); antimotility agents also avoided.

Supportive care: careful fluid management (often volume-depleted at presentation but progress to oliguric failure), red cell transfusion as needed, dialysis in ~half, avoid platelet transfusion unless actively bleeding.

cards.front: The most common cyanotic congenital heart disease overall is [___].
cards.context: The classic cyanotic lesion, presenting after the neonatal period as the right-ventricular outflow obstruction tightens. Its four components: VSD, overriding aorta, RV outflow obstruction, and RV hypertrophy.

cards.front: A five-week-old with progressive non-bilious vomiting has low chloride and potassium after repeated gastric losses. The expected acid-base disturbance is metabolic [___].
cards.context:
Repeated vomiting removes gastric acid. The biochemical disturbance becomes more marked with prolonged symptoms, so an early presentation may lack the classic pattern.

Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities before pyloromyotomy. Stabilisation precedes the definitive operation.

cards.front: A 20-month-old with three weeks of fevers, weight loss, and refusal to walk has a firm, irregular abdominal mass extending past the midline; CT shows calcification within it. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
Three specifics converge: extension past the midline (paraspinal sympathetic origin), calcification on CT (common here, rare in Wilms'), and a systemically unwell child.

Refusal to walk signals marrow or bone metastases.

A smooth flank mass in a well child, without calcification, would point instead to the renal tumour of this age group.

cards.front: After a positive newborn screen for cystic fibrosis, the standard physiological confirmatory investigation is a [___].
cards.context: The test measures sweat chloride, reflecting impaired CFTR function. A positive screening result needs diagnostic confirmation and specialist interpretation.

cards.front: A child with haemophilia A receives emicizumab. Which routine assay should the laboratory avoid using to monitor factor VIII activity? [___]
cards.context:
Emicizumab changes phospholipid-dependent clotting assays, so the usual aPTT can look misleading. The laboratory and haemophilia team need to know that the child receives emicizumab.

Do not use a routine aPTT to monitor factor VIII activity or an inhibitor in a child receiving emicizumab; follow the specialist testing plan instead.

cards.front: CPK on an older request form or slide is the same enzyme as [___], the muscle enzyme released when muscle breaks down.
cards.context:
Purely a naming trap, and worth thirty seconds because the two names appear interchangeably on slides, request forms and in exam stems.

CPK stands for creatine phosphokinase — the older name for the same enzyme now usually written CK, creatine kinase. There is no difference in the test: both mean the muscle enzyme released when muscle fibres break down.

So an instruction ending 'check CPK' is telling you to confirm that a raised transaminase is coming from muscle rather than liver.

cards.front: When bile flow is obstructed (cholestasis) in a child, the two LFT enzymes that rise are [___] and GGT, rather than the hepatocellular ALT/AST.
cards.context:
ALP and GGT mark the bile-duct (cholestatic) side of the panel and climb when bile can't drain (e.g. biliary atresia in a jaundiced infant).

The trap in paediatrics: ALP also rises from growing bone, so a high ALP is only cholestatic if GGT rises alongside it; isolated high ALP in a well child is often normal growth.

cards.front: Newborn screening for cystic fibrosis uses IRT (raised by pancreatic damage); confirm with sweat chloride >[___] mmol/L.
cards.context:
The CF screening pathway has three steps. Step 1 — newborn heel-prick measures immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT), raised because early pancreatic damage releases trypsinogen into circulation.

Step 2 — if IRT is elevated, CFTR gene testing screens for common mutations.

Step 3 — sweat chloride confirms the diagnosis. Pilocarpine iontophoresis stimulates sweating and chloride is measured: >60 mmol/L = CF, 30-59 = intermediate (repeat or genetic), <30 = unlikely.

cards.front: Mediastinal air that elevates the thymic lobes produces the [___].
cards.context:
In neonatal pneumomediastinum, air tracks beneath the thymus and lifts its lobes away from the cardiac shadow.

Air lifts the thymic lobes away from the heart, creating the spinnaker-sail appearance. Angel-wing is another name for this neonatal pneumomediastinum sign.

cards.front: Using the NAC Spirometry Handbook baseline-relative criterion, a child’s FEV1 must rise by at least [___]% after bronchodilator.
cards.context: The denominator is the pre-bronchodilator reading. The Australian Asthma Handbook also describes a separate criterion based on predicted FEV1; these percentages are not interchangeable.

cards.front: Persistent asthma in a 6-11-year-old means daytime symptoms at least [___] per week, night-time symptoms at least twice per month, or symptoms that restrict activity or sleep.
cards.context:
These are eTG's criteria, and any ONE of the three is enough — daytime frequency, night-time frequency, or functional impact.

Attribute the daytime number: AAH sets its preventer trigger at daytime symptoms twice per week or more, where eTG's persistent threshold is once per week.

Both share the night-time threshold of twice per month, and AAH adds any exacerbation needing systemic corticosteroids in the past 12 months.

cards.front: A 15-year-old with normal growth velocity, delayed bone age, and a parent who was a late bloomer most likely has [___] delay of growth and puberty.
cards.context: Constitutional delay is the normal-variant late-bloomer pattern: growth velocity remains normal, bone age lags behind chronological age, and the extra growing time preserves a normal adult-height prediction.

cards.front: Main drivers of adolescent morbidity: mental health, injury, chronic illness, and [___] behaviours; screen with the HEEADSSS psychosocial tool (Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Mood, Safety).
cards.context:
The epidemiology flips in adolescence: most morbidity and mortality now comes from behaviour and mental health (suicide, motor-vehicle injury, substance use), not the infections that dominate early childhood.

That is why a symptom-focused interview misses the real risks — you have to actively screen the psychosocial domains with HEEADSSS.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: Recounting an event, predicting the next part of a familiar story, naming colours, catching a large ball and unbuttoning fit the [___]-year profile.
cards.context:
The four-year profile adds narrative and sequence: telling one event from the day and predicting what comes next in a familiar story.

It also includes naming colours, catching a large ball, unbuttoning and holding a pencil between fingers and thumb rather than a fist.

Do not inflate the final observation into a claim that a mature tripod grasp is mandatory.

cards.front: An overweight adolescent has referred knee pain, an out-turned leg and restricted hip rotation. Until orthopaedic review, the activity status is [___].
cards.context:
Hip pathology can present as knee pain. An overweight adolescent with out-toeing and restricted hip rotation should be treated as possible SUFE until assessed.

All suspected SUFE needs urgent orthopaedic assessment. Keep the child non-weight-bearing in bed or a wheelchair; crutches still load the unstable hip.

cards.front: A displaced distal radius fracture can cause early compartment syndrome (rising pressure in the forearm fascial space) and, if the physis is injured, late [___].
cards.context: The SAQ asks for one early and one late complication of a distal forearm fracture. Early = a surgical emergency from swelling in the closed forearm space; late = the growth plate is the vulnerable structure in children.

cards.front: A common paediatric Gram-negative coccobacillus is Haemophilus [___].
cards.context:
Haemophilus influenzae is the stock paediatric Gram-negative coccobacillus (otitis/sinusitis; historically Hib epiglottitis).

Contrast: meningococcus = Gram-negative diplococcus; pneumococcus = Gram-positive lancet diplococcus.

cards.front: LARC methods (implants, IUDs) are recommended first-line in adolescents because efficacy is independent of daily [___]; pair with condoms for STI protection.
cards.context:
LARC (Implanon 3y, copper IUD 5-10y, Mirena 5-8y) is first-line for adolescents because efficacy is independent of daily compliance. Real-world failure <1% per year vs ~9% for daily OCPs (missed pills).

IUDs are safe in nulliparous patients — they don't affect future fertility or increase ectopic risk. Counsel adolescents about LARC explicitly; many only learn of it when an adult assumes they 'wouldn't want one'.

cards.front: Neonatal purulent eye discharge on day 2-5 of life is most likely caused by [___].
cards.context:
Timing of neonatal conjunctivitis tracks the organism's incubation: chemical in first 24 h, gonococcal at day 2-5, chlamydial day 5-14, HSV beyond a week.

Sight-threatening: gonococcus can penetrate intact corneal epithelium and cause corneal ulceration, perforation, blindness within 24-48 h.

Always send Gram stain + culture before antibiotics.

cards.front: Bronchiolitis management is supportive (oxygen/hydration); [___] are NOT routinely recommended because obstruction is mechanical, not bronchospasm.
cards.context:
Bronchiolitis is viral small-airway inflammation with mucus plugging, not bronchospasm.

Treatment is supportive: oxygen below 90% if ≥6 weeks and low-risk, or below 92% if younger/high-risk; NG/IV fluids if feeding is inadequate.

Escalate respiratory support to HFNC, then NIV or intubation if the infant becomes exhausted.

cards.front: Current hepatitis B infection is marked by a positive [___]; anti-HBs alone means immunity, including after vaccine.
cards.context: Anti-HBs is immunity. HBsAg is virus currently present. Vaccination produces anti-HBs without HBsAg or anti-HBc.

cards.front: Mid-parental height = (father + mother ± 13) / 2 cm (add for boys, subtract for girls); target range around the predicted height is ± [___] cm.
cards.context:
Mid-parental height predicts adult-height genetic potential — (father + mother ± 13)/2 cm (+13 boys, −13 girls), target ±8.5 cm. The ±13 correction goes INSIDE the average (shifts parental mean 6.5 cm), not onto it.

Use to interpret growth chart positioning — 5th-percentile child with mid-parental target on 3rd is genetically small (no pathology); same child with parents on 50th is likely growth failure.

Combine with bone age (left wrist X-ray): delayed + short = constitutional delay; normal age + short with short parents = familial; delayed + short with normal parents = work up GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, coeliac.

cards.front: Main drivers of adolescent morbidity: [___] health, injury, chronic illness, and risk-taking behaviours; screen with the HEEADSSS psychosocial tool (Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Mood, Safety).
cards.context:
The epidemiology flips in adolescence: most morbidity and mortality now comes from behaviour and mental health (suicide, motor-vehicle injury, substance use), not the infections that dominate early childhood.

That is why a symptom-focused interview misses the real risks — you have to actively screen the psychosocial domains with HEEADSSS.

cards.front: A 7-year-old girl has pubic hair, axillary hair and adult-type body odour, but no breast development; her LH and FSH are prepubertal and bone age is near-normal. The most likely diagnosis is premature [___].
cards.context:
Pubic/axillary hair, body odour and acne are adrenal-androgen effects and can appear years before true puberty.

The trap is calling this precocious puberty: true puberty requires gonadal (HPG-axis) activation, so here LH/FSH stay prepubertal, bone age is near-normal, and there is no breast or testicular development.

Recognising the benign mimic avoids unnecessary work-up.

cards.front: In cystic fibrosis, the defective cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel produces [___], dehydrated airway secretions; impaired mucociliary clearance drives chronic infection and progressive bronchiectasis.
cards.context:
CFTR normally exports chloride into airway lumen, drawing water with it to keep mucus hydrated for cilial clearance.

Once bronchiectasis develops, the cycle is self-sustaining.

cards.front: Most common bacterial pneumonia organism in children is Streptococcus pneumoniae; [___] causes 'walking pneumonia' in older children.
cards.context:
The organism shifts with age: Strep pneumoniae dominates classic lobar pneumonia (acute fever, focal consolidation), so amoxicillin is empirical first-line.

Mycoplasma becomes important in school-age children — its 'walking pneumonia' is more gradual with dry cough and patchy changes, and being atypical (no cell wall) it needs a macrolide, not amoxicillin.

cards.front: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in a 4–10-year-old boy is called [___].
cards.context:
Perthes follows interruption of blood supply to the developing femoral head, producing avascular necrosis, fragmentation and later remodelling.

The age band is the discriminator: think Perthes in a 4–10-year-old boy with an insidious limp or hip pain referred to the knee; an overweight 10–14-year-old instead raises concern for slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

cards.front: Paediatric Hb reference ranges are [___]-dependent rather than fixed; the lower limit of normal for a 1-5 year old sits around 110 g/L.
cards.context:
The trap: a Hb that looks low against the adult range may be normal for a child. Reference ranges shift with age — high at birth, a physiological trough in infancy, then a slow climb toward adult values through puberty.

Always interpret a paediatric Hb against the age-specific range, which the exam will provide; never anchor to the adult ~130-140 figure.

cards.front: Single-dose oral [___] (0.15 mg/kg wafer) reduces vomiting in paediatric gastroenteritis and the need for IV fluids; give before attempting oral rehydration.
cards.context:
Single-dose ondansetron wafer (0.15 mg/kg, max 8 mg) halves persistent vomiting in mild-to-moderate paediatric gastroenteritis and reduces the need for IV fluids and admission (Cochrane evidence is strong).

Practical: give the wafer first, wait 15-20 minutes, then start oral rehydration with small frequent volumes. Avoid in infants <6 months and known long QT syndrome; one dose is usually enough.

cards.front: An alert toddler with gastroenteritis has moderate dehydration but cannot drink enough. There is no shock or suspected bowel obstruction. Oral rehydration solution can next be delivered through a [___] tube.
cards.context:
The gut can still absorb fluid when a child cannot drink enough voluntarily. Nasogastric delivery provides an enteral route without relying on repeated sips.

Shock requires intravenous resuscitation. Reassess hydration and response regularly rather than treating the route choice as the end of the assessment.

cards.front: Neonatal age and renal or hepatic impairment may require antibiotic dose or [___] adjustment.
cards.context:
The prescribed agent is only half the decision. Dose and interval can change with gestational and postnatal age, renal clearance, hepatic function, weight and the severity or compartment of infection.

RCH explicitly flags neonates and children with renal or hepatic impairment for adjustment; use a current paediatric formulary rather than scaling an adult schedule.

cards.front: An infant with a persistently undescended testis has been referred for surgery. The preferred age window for orchidopexy is [___] months.
cards.context: Referral needs to precede the operation, so an empty scrotum in early infancy should not be left until the first birthday. Earlier repair reduces prolonged exposure of the testis to body temperature.

cards.front: Recurrent painful clusters of vesicles at the border of the lip ('cold sores') are herpes [___].
cards.context: Herpes labialis is recurrent HSV-1 reactivation, often triggered by sunlight, illness, or stress. Topical or oral aciclovir helps if started in the tingling prodrome.

reference.title: ASCIA-TAPID Consensus Guideline: Diagnosis, Management and Transplantation of SCID in Australia and New Zealand

cards.front: TORCH organisms typically reach the fetus by crossing the [___] during pregnancy.
cards.context:
The unifying mechanism: the organism crosses the placenta and infects the fetus during development, rather than the baby catching something after birth.

That is why the damage is structural — organs are being built while the infection is happening — and why the timing in pregnancy matters so much.

Early infection tends to cause more severe malformation; later infection causes more active inflammatory disease. Herpes simplex is the exception that proves the rule, and is dealt with separately below.

cards.front: Of 100 children who have a simple febrile convulsion, only about [___] will later develop epilepsy.
cards.context: A brief, generalised convulsion with full recovery is a simple febrile convulsion. It only slightly raises later epilepsy risk, so reassure rather than prescribe long-term anticonvulsant prophylaxis.

cards.front: Treat a paediatric seizure as status epilepticus once it has lasted [___] (or recurrent without recovery) — do not wait for a longer traditional cut-off.
cards.context: Same seizure numbers, different probe: status epilepticus is the 5-minute clock that triggers benzodiazepines.

cards.front: Australia diagnoses about [___] new cancers per 100,000 children aged 0–14 each year.
cards.context: AIHW data for 2011–2015 report about 16 new cancers per 100,000 Australian children aged 0–14 each year. Leukaemia, especially ALL, is the commonest category.

cards.front: Three immediate steps for a severely unwell child with pneumonia are [___], IV fluids, and IV antibiotics.
cards.context:
A severely unwell or septic child (e.g. asplenic, or with high RR, hypoxia, poor perfusion) needs resuscitation alongside diagnosis.

The three immediate steps are the ABC-led sepsis bundle: oxygen, IV fluids, and prompt IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) — don't wait for imaging.

cards.front: School-age flexural itch in a child with asthma or hay fever is [___] until a mimic is proven.
cards.context:
Infant eczema often sits on the face and extensors; after infancy it prefers the elbow and knee flexures.

Itch plus an atopic personal or family history is the clinical diagnosis — you do not need a serum IgE to start emollients.

cards.front: A 5-year-old boy climbs up his own thighs to stand and waddles when he walks. Weakness of the hip girdle like this usually comes from disease of the [___] itself.
cards.context:
Gowers' sign and a waddling gait are the bedside face of a weak pelvic girdle, and a raised creatine kinase then points to a muscular dystrophy.

In myopathy, reflexes fade only in proportion to the weakness and sensation is normal; sensory loss or early lost ankle reflexes point to nerve instead.

Rule of thumb: proximal means muscle, distal means nerve, fatigable with droopy eyelids means the junction, and fasciculations point to the anterior horn.

cards.front: A facial port-wine stain raises concern for Sturge-Weber when it involves the [___] division of the trigeminal nerve.
cards.context:
NOT EVERY FACIAL PORT-WINE STAIN IS STURGE-WEBER. The great majority are isolated capillary malformations with no intracranial involvement at all, and telling a family otherwise is a serious thing to get wrong.

The risk attaches to the distribution. Involvement of the OPHTHALMIC (V1) division — forehead and upper eyelid — is what associates with a leptomeningeal angioma.

A stain confined to V2 or V3 carries little or no such risk. So the question at the cot side is not 'is there a port-wine stain' but 'does it involve the forehead and upper eyelid'.

cards.front: Patching the stronger eye during the visual critical period treats [___].
cards.context: Amblyopia is a developmental problem in the visual pathway, not structural eye damage. Occluding the stronger eye forces use of the weaker eye while childhood visual plasticity remains.

cards.front: The cyanotic lesion behind a boot-shaped heart on CXR — the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease — is [___].
cards.context:
Reverse cue for the same fact: the CXR silhouette. RV hypertrophy tips the apex upward while the small pulmonary trunk hollows the upper left heart border, producing the classic boot.

Pulmonary vascular markings are reduced — the outflow obstruction limits lung blood flow — separating it from the plethoric left-to-right shunts.

cards.front: Bronchiolitis management is [___] only — bronchodilators and steroids have no proven benefit.
cards.context:
Bronchiolitis is small-airway plugging by sloughed epithelium and mucus, not bronchospasm.

Care is supportive: minimal handling, oxygen below 90% if ≥6 weeks and low-risk or below 92% if younger/high-risk, and NG/IV fluids if feeding is impaired.

cards.front: Over 80% of paediatric osteomyelitis is caused by [___] aureus.
cards.context: Haematogenous paediatric osteomyelitis is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus. Early plain films miss marrow change — MRI is the early imaging of choice.

cards.front: A child needed feeding support for neonatal hypotonia but later developed persistent food-seeking and excessive appetite. This change in feeding pattern suggests [___].
cards.context:
Poor sucking and low tone can dominate infancy; excessive appetite develops later in childhood. The sequence is more informative than obesity alone.

Hypothalamic dysfunction impairs satiety, so food-seeking is part of the condition rather than simple lack of willpower.

cards.front: The mainstay of eczema management, applied regularly even when the skin is clear, is [___].
cards.context:
Emollients are moisturisers and the foundation of every eczema plan: used liberally and continued even when the skin looks clear, because they restore the defective skin barrier rather than treating inflammation.

Topical steroids are added for flares on top of this, never instead of it.

cards.front: Early introduction of allergenic foods (peanut, egg) via [___] route promotes tolerance before transcutaneous sensitisation; supported by LEAP and EAT studies.
cards.context:
The skin barrier hypothesis: cutaneous (eczema-mediated) exposure primes Th2 sensitisation; oral exposure promotes tolerance. LEAP means Learning Early About Peanut Allergy; EAT means Enquiring About Tolerance.

 These trials informed the shift away from delaying common food allergens. Australian guidelines now recommend introduction at around 6 months, when the infant is developmentally ready, rather than delay.

cards.front: NF2 is defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, so it presents with [___] rather than with the skin findings of NF1.
cards.context:
NF1 AND NF2 ARE DIFFERENT DISEASES, not mild and severe versions of one. Different gene, different chromosome, different clinical problem. Conflating them is the commonest error on this topic.

NF1 (chromosome 17, neurofibromin) is the skin-and-nerve one: café-au-lait macules, freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic glioma. It is what people mean when they say 'neurofibromatosis'.

NF2 (chromosome 22, merlin) barely involves the skin. Its defining lesion is BILATERAL VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMAS, so it presents as hearing loss, tinnitus or imbalance in a young adult — not as a childhood rash.

cards.front: Strabismus affects ~[___]% of children; untreated risks amblyopia (vision suppression in the misaligned eye).
cards.context:
Strabismus (eye misalignment) affects ~2% of children. Risk factors: family history, prematurity, refractive error (commonly hyperopia → accommodative esotropia), neurological disorders.

Untreated strabismus causes amblyopia (vision suppression in the misaligned eye) — refer to ophthalmology by age 4-6 months for any persistent misalignment.

cards.front: In uncomplicated paediatric community-acquired pneumonia, RCH uses [___] first line; a macrolide is reserved for a defined atypical indication.
cards.context:
Macrolides are used for defined indications such as pertussis and selected atypical respiratory infection.

RCH still uses amoxicillin for uncomplicated paediatric community-acquired pneumonia because pneumococcus and viruses dominate.

A possibility of Mycoplasma does not automatically make azithromycin the default for every mild cough and infiltrate.

cards.front: An 8-year-old's systolic floor on the RCH acceptable-range chart is [___] mmHg, whereas the APLS formula gives 86 — the formula is deliberately the more conservative of the two.
cards.context:
This is the discrepancy that catches people who have learned the formula as though it were the observation chart.

The two tools disagree by a few mmHg at every age in the 1-10 band, always in the same direction — the formula is the more conservative, flagging the child a little earlier. That is deliberate in a resuscitation aid.

What you must not do is quote the formula's output as the fifth centile. If a chart is in front of you, the chart wins.

cards.front: Recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infections suggest [___] complement deficiency (C5-C9).
cards.context:
C5-C9 form the membrane attack complex, the only mechanism that can directly lyse encapsulated Gram-negatives like Neisseria.

Workup: CH50 (screens classical pathway) + AH50 if alternative-pathway disease suspected; specific components follow. These children need MenB + ACWY vaccines, may need long-term penicillin prophylaxis.

cards.front: A newborn is visibly jaundiced on the first day of life. The usual cause is haemolysis from Rh or ABO [___].
cards.context: Very early jaundice triggers an urgent bilirubin and haemolysis work-up rather than reassurance. The usual culprit is brisk haemolysis from Rh or ABO incompatibility.
